title: "Rerandomization"
description: >
  Randomising once can hand you arms that differ on the very things you were
  trying to hold constant. Rerandomization refuses those splits before the
  experiment starts.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import json, pathlib
from IPython.display import HTML, display

rng = np.random.default_rng(20260824)

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor":  "white",
    "axes.facecolor":    "white",
    "axes.edgecolor":    "#9aa4ad",
    "axes.linewidth":    0.9,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "axes.axisbelow":    True,
    "grid.color":        "#ccd4db",
    "grid.linewidth":    0.8,
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.titlesize":    12,
    "axes.titleweight":  "semibold",
    "axes.labelsize":    11,
    "xtick.labelsize":   10,
    "ytick.labelsize":   10,
    "xtick.color":       "#3f4850",
    "ytick.color":       "#3f4850",
    "legend.frameon":    False,
    "legend.fontsize":   10,
    "font.size":         11,
})

C = {
    "blue":   "#2c6e9b",
    "orange": "#d1743a",
    "green":  "#4f8f63",
    "red":    "#b5483d",
    "grey":   "#9aa3ab",
    "dark":   "#2c4a63",
}

# The running example from the Mahalanobis article: height and weight,
# correlated at 0.7.
mu_hw = np.array([170.0, 75.0])
sd_hw = np.array([10.0, 15.0])
S_hw  = np.outer(sd_hw, sd_hw) * np.array([[1.0, 0.7], [0.7, 1.0]])
```

You randomise a few hundred people into two arms, and then you look at the
baseline table. The treatment group is a year older. It is also, because age and
blood pressure travel together, slightly hypertensive. Nothing has gone wrong —
this is what randomisation does, and it will happen to roughly one experiment in
twenty for any covariate you care to check. But you now get to spend the rest of
the study explaining it, and the imbalance sits in your standard errors whether
you explain it or not.

Rerandomization takes the obvious way out. Randomisation is cheap, so draw a
split, measure how unbalanced it is, and if it is unacceptable, throw it away and
draw another. Keep going until you get one you would be happy to defend. The
result is still a genuinely random assignment — you simply drew it from a smaller
pool of good ones. All of the work happens before a single unit is treated, and
the only cost is CPU time.

## How it works

The measure of imbalance is the Mahalanobis distance from
[the previous article](../mahalanobis-distance/), which is what lets you collapse
a whole covariate table into one number without double-counting the covariates
that say the same thing.

Concretely, with $N$ units, $k$ covariates and two equal arms:

::: {.keybox}
1. Compute the covariate covariance matrix $S$ **once**, from all $N$ units.
2. Draw a candidate split. Take the two arms' covariate mean vectors,
   $\bar X_T$ and $\bar X_C$.
3. The imbalance score is the squared Mahalanobis distance between those two
   mean vectors, scaled by $N/4$:
   $$
   M \;=\; \frac{N}{4}\,(\bar X_T - \bar X_C)^{\!\top} S^{-1} (\bar X_T - \bar X_C).
   $$
4. If $M \le a$, keep the split. Otherwise discard it and go back to step 2.
:::

Step 1 is the one worth flagging: $S$ describes the pool of units, not the split,
so it never changes as you redraw. Compute it once, outside the loop, along with
whatever factorisation you use to apply $S^{-1}$. Every later iteration is then
just a pair of means and a quadratic form.

The $N/4$ is not decoration. Under complete randomisation the mean-difference
vector has covariance $\tfrac{4}{N} S$, so that factor is exactly what turns $M$
into the squared Mahalanobis distance of the imbalance from its own null
distribution — which is what makes the next section possible.

## Choosing the threshold

Because $M$ is a squared Mahalanobis distance of an approximately normal
$k$-vector, it follows a chi-square distribution on $k$ degrees of freedom. So
the threshold is a chi-square quantile. To accept a proportion $p_a$ of draws,

$$
a = F^{-1}_{\chi^2_k}(p_a), \qquad \text{accept if } M \le a .
$$

The expected number of draws before one is accepted is $1/p_a$. That is the
entire cost model: a 1-in-1,000 threshold costs about 1,000 draws.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-thresholds
#| echo: false

rows = []
for p_a_ in [0.5, 0.1, 0.05, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001]:
    for k_ in [2, 5, 10, 20]:
        rows.append({"p_a": p_a_, "k": k_,
                     "a": stats.chi2.ppf(p_a_, k_)})
thr = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="p_a", columns="k", values="a")
thr.columns = [f"k = {c}" for c in thr.columns]
thr.insert(0, "expected draws", [round(1 / x) for x in thr.index])
thr.round(3)
```

: Threshold $a$ to use for a given acceptance rate $p_a$ (rows) and number of covariates $k$ (columns). Accept a split when $M \le a$. The second column is the average number of draws you will get through before one is accepted. {#tbl-thresholds}

## A budget instead of a threshold

Picking $p_a$ means committing to an unbounded loop: you will *probably* accept
within a few thousand draws, but nothing guarantees it. The alternative is to
fix a budget — draw 10,000 splits, keep the single best one — which runs in
known time and requires no threshold at all.

These are not the same procedure, and the difference goes the way most people
guess wrong. Drawing $B$ and keeping the best is **worse** than thresholding at
$p_a = 1/B$, because the winner of a tournament of $B$ is not guaranteed to clear
the 1-in-$B$ bar: it misses it about $(1 - 1/B)^B \approx 37\%$ of the time.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-budget
#| echo: false

rows = []
for k_ in [2, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
    a_ = stats.chi2.ppf(1e-4, k_)
    v_thresh = stats.chi2.cdf(a_, k_ + 2) / stats.chi2.cdf(a_, k_)
    draws = stats.chi2.rvs(k_, size=(3000, 10_000), random_state=rng)
    v_best = draws.min(axis=1).mean() / k_
    rows.append({"covariates k": k_,
                 "threshold at p_a = 1/10,000": f"{v_thresh:.5f}",
                 "best of 10,000 draws": f"{v_best:.5f}",
                 "ratio": f"{v_best / v_thresh:.2f}x"})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("covariates k")
```

: Residual imbalance variance $v$ under the two schemes, as a fraction of what complete randomisation leaves. Lower is better. Best-of-10,000 is never better than thresholding at 1 in 10,000, but the gap closes quickly as covariates are added. {#tbl-budget}

With two covariates the budget approach leaves twice the imbalance variance. By
ten covariates the penalty is 11%, and by twenty it is 6% — small enough that
the predictable runtime is usually worth it. **If you have more than a handful of
covariates, picking a budget you can afford and keeping the best draw is a
perfectly respectable design**, and it removes the one genuinely awkward
parameter. Just record that this is what you did, because the inference has to
match the scheme you actually ran.

## The acceptance region

With two covariates you can see the thing. Each dot below is one candidate
split, placed at its pair of covariate mean differences. The cloud is tilted
because height and weight are correlated: a split that over-represents tall
people over-represents heavy ones too.

The acceptance region is the ellipse. At a 5% acceptance rate it is so much
smaller than the cloud that it is barely a smudge at the origin, which is the
honest visual point — so drag to zoom in on it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-acceptance-zoom
#| echo: false

N = 200
n_T = N // 2
B = 8000

Xrr = rng.multivariate_normal(mu_hw, S_hw, N)
S_rr = np.cov(Xrr, rowvar=False, ddof=1)
cov_d = (4 / N) * S_rr

idx = np.argsort(rng.random((B, N)), axis=1)[:, :n_T]
s_mat = -np.ones((B, N))
np.put_along_axis(s_mat, idx, 1.0, axis=1)
d_all = (2 / N) * (s_mat @ Xrr)

p_a_main = 0.05
payload = {
    "pts":  np.round(d_all, 4).tolist(),
    "Cinv": np.linalg.inv(cov_d).tolist(),
    "L":    np.linalg.cholesky(cov_d).tolist(),
    "sd":   np.sqrt(np.diag(cov_d)).tolist(),
    "aMain": float(stats.chi2.ppf(p_a_main, 2)),
    "rings": [{"a": float(stats.chi2.ppf(q, 2)), "main": q == p_a_main}
              for q in (0.50, 0.20, 0.05, 0.01)],
    "xlab": "imbalance in mean height (cm)",
    "ylab": "imbalance in mean weight (kg)",
    "colors": {"grey": C["grey"], "green": C["green"], "dark": C["dark"],
               "grid": "#ccd4db", "axis": "#9aa4ad", "tick": "#3f4850"},
}

js = pathlib.Path("acceptance-zoom.js").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
js = js.replace("__ID__", "rz-accept").replace("__DATA__", json.dumps(payload))

display(HTML("""
<style>
.rerand-zoom { margin: 1.2rem 0 1.6rem; text-align:left; }
.rerand-zoom canvas { display:block; width:100%; touch-action:manipulation; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-readout { font-size:.82rem; color:#5b6570; text-align:center;
  margin:.35rem 0 .7rem; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-readout b { color:#21252b; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-sep { margin:0 .6rem; opacity:.45; }
.rerand-zoom input[type=range] { width:100%; margin:0; accent-color:#2c6e9b; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels { display:flex; justify-content:space-between;
  font-size:.82rem; color:#8a929a; margin-top:.3rem; padding:0 9px;
  text-align:left; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels span { cursor:pointer; flex:1; text-align:left; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels span:nth-child(2) { text-align:center; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels span:nth-child(3) { text-align:right; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels span.rz-on { color:#2c4a63; font-weight:600; }
</style>
<div class="rerand-zoom" id="rz-accept">
  <canvas></canvas>
  <div class="rz-readout"></div>
  <input type="range" min="0" max="1000" step="1" value="0"
         aria-label="Zoom level, from every draw to the acceptance region">
  <div class="rz-labels">
    <span data-at="0">every draw</span>
    <span data-at="500">3&times; zoom</span>
    <span data-at="1000">10&times; &mdash; the 5% region</span>
  </div>
</div>
<script>""" + js + "</script>"))
```

Zoomed all the way in, the green dots are the splits you would have kept. Notice
that they are not the ones where both imbalances are near zero — they are the
ones inside a *tilted* ellipse, which tolerates a larger height imbalance when
weight is imbalanced the same way, and is strict about the two disagreeing. That
tilt is $\Sigma^{-1}$ doing its job, and it is the reason the criterion is a
Mahalanobis distance rather than a sum of squared z-scores.

## How much does it buy you?

Fix one covariate — say age — and ask how much its arm-to-arm difference bounces
around from experiment to experiment.

- $\operatorname{Var}_{\text{CR}}$ is that variance under **complete
  randomisation**: draw once, accept whatever you get.
- $\operatorname{Var}_{\text{RR}}$ is the same variance under
  **rerandomization**: draw repeatedly, keep only splits with $M \le a$.

Rerandomization can only shrink it, and Morgan and Rubin showed it shrinks by
the same factor for every covariate at once:

::: {.keybox}
$$
v_a \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\text{RR}}}{\operatorname{Var}_{\text{CR}}}
      \;=\; \frac{P(\chi^2_{k+2} \le a)}{P(\chi^2_{k} \le a)} .
$$
:::

Read $v_a$ as "the fraction of the imbalance that survives". $v_a = 1$ means
rerandomization bought nothing; $v_a = 0.05$ means 95% of the imbalance variance
is gone.

The one number worth memorising is what a 1-in-10,000 threshold delivers as the
covariate count grows.

```{python}
#| label: fig-variance-reduction
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Fraction of the imbalance variance that survives rerandomization at a 1-in-10,000 acceptance rate, as the number of covariates grows. Balancing a handful of covariates removes almost all of it; balancing fifty removes less than half, for the same 10,000 draws."
#| fig-height: 3.9

ks = np.arange(1, 61)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 3.9))
for p_a_, col, lab in [(1e-4, C["blue"], "$p_a = 1/10{,}000$"),
                       (1e-3, C["orange"], "$p_a = 1/1{,}000$")]:
    a_g = stats.chi2.ppf(p_a_, ks)
    ax.plot(ks, stats.chi2.cdf(a_g, ks + 2) / stats.chi2.cdf(a_g, ks),
            color=col, lw=2.2, label=lab)
ax.set_xlabel("number of covariates $k$")
ax.set_ylabel("$v_a$ = fraction of imbalance left")
ax.set_title("The benefit erodes as you add covariates")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlim(1, 60)
ax.legend(loc="lower right")

for k_ in (5, 20, 50):
    a_ = stats.chi2.ppf(1e-4, k_)
    v_ = stats.chi2.cdf(a_, k_ + 2) / stats.chi2.cdf(a_, k_)
    ax.scatter([k_], [v_], s=45, color=C["blue"], zorder=5,
               edgecolor="white", lw=1)
    ax.annotate(f"$k$={k_}: {v_:.0%}", (k_, v_), textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=(7, 7), fontsize=9.5, color=C["blue"])

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Five covariates at 1-in-10,000 leaves about 1% of the imbalance. Fifty leaves
40%. The budget does not scale: every covariate you add has to be balanced
simultaneously, and the acceptance region shrinks in every direction at once.
**Do not throw covariates at the criterion because you have them** — each one
you add dilutes the balance achieved on the ones you actually care about.

::: {.callout-important}
## Balance is not the goal; precision is

The variance of your treatment effect estimate falls by a factor of
$1 - (1 - v_a)R^2$, where $R^2$ is the squared multiple correlation between the
outcome and the covariates you balanced.

That $R^2$ term is doing at least as much work as $v_a$. If the covariates do not
predict the outcome, perfect balance on them buys you exactly nothing. Choosing
*which* covariates to balance matters more than choosing how hard to balance
them — and it is the decision people spend the least time on.
:::

## Inference after rerandomization

*Outline — to be written.*

Rerandomization changes the design, so it changes what "by chance" means. Two
positions to reconcile:

1. **Adjust for the balancing covariates in the analysis.** This is what most
   practitioners do: regress the outcome on treatment plus the covariates used
   in the design. It is simple, familiar, and largely self-correcting.
2. **Use the rerandomization distribution directly.** Li, Ding and Rubin (2018)
   show that the unadjusted difference in means is no longer asymptotically
   normal after rerandomization — it is a normal plus a truncated-normal term,
   because the design has removed exactly the part of the imbalance that the
   covariates explain. A conventional $t$-test is therefore *conservative*:
   intervals are too wide, and you lose the precision the design just bought.

Planned content: why the two views mostly agree when the analysis adjusts for
the same covariates used in the design; how to run a randomisation test that
redraws under the same acceptance rule (including the best-of-$B$ variant, where
the rule is not a simple threshold); and when the truncated-normal correction is
worth the trouble.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Use the covariate values as they stood at the moment of splitting

This is the question I could not find answered cleanly anywhere, so to state it
plainly: the analysis must use the **pre-randomisation** values of the balancing
covariates, not their latest values.

Suppose you ran a development experiment across villages and balanced on village
population. By the end of the study, populations have changed — and if the
intervention worked, it may well have *caused* some of that change, through
migration or falling child mortality. Adjusting for end-of-study population
would then be conditioning on something the treatment affected. That is
post-treatment bias: it removes part of the very effect you are trying to
measure, and it can flip the sign of an estimate.

The design argument points the same way. The randomisation distribution is
defined by the acceptance rule, and that rule was evaluated against the baseline
numbers. Those are the values that determine which splits could have occurred,
so those are the values the analysis has to condition on. Freeze your covariate
table when you draw the split, and keep it.
:::

## Covariate adjustment as an alternative

*Outline — to be written.*

If you are going to regress the outcome on the covariates anyway, why bother
balancing them in the design? Planned content:

- **What adjustment alone gets you.** Regression can remove imbalance after the
  fact, and for a linear outcome model it recovers most of what rerandomization
  would have delivered.
- **Why the design stage still earns its keep.** Adjustment is a modelling
  choice made after you have seen the data, which invites specification search;
  balance is a property of the assignment, fixed before any outcome exists.
  Severe imbalance also makes adjustment an extrapolation rather than an
  interpolation.
- **The honest comparison.** A simulation over linear outcomes, non-linear
  outcomes, and a case where the covariates are irrelevant — which is where
  rerandomization has the least to offer and adjustment quietly costs degrees of
  freedom.

## Practical notes and failure modes

**Feasibility at small $N$.** There are only $\binom{N}{N/2}$ distinct equal
splits. That is astronomically large for $N = 200$, but for $N = 20$ it is
184,756, and an acceptance rate of $10^{-6}$ is then not merely slow but
impossible. Check that $p_a \binom{N}{N/2} \gg 1$.

**More covariates is not free.** A correlated covariate gets no extra weight in
$M$, but it does raise $k$, which shrinks the benefit available at any budget.

**Every covariate is treated as equally important.** $M$ is invariant to
rescaling, which is a virtue for units and a limitation for priorities. If some
covariates genuinely matter more, use tiered rerandomization (Morgan and Rubin,
2015), which applies separate thresholds to groups of covariates in order of
importance.

**Keep the accepted split reproducible.** Record the seed, the covariate table,
the encoding and the threshold. $S$ is computed from the data at hand, so
changing the covariate set changes the metric and therefore the accepted split.
